'''''Juniperus phoenicea''''', the '''Phoenicean juniper''' or '''Arâr''',<ref>ambiguous Arabic name also given to ''[[Tetraclinis articulata]]''</ref> is a species of [[juniper]] found in the western [[Mediterranean basin|Mediterranean region]].

==Description==
''Juniperus phoenicea'' is a large evergreen [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] reaching {{convert|5|-|8|m|abbr=off}} tall, with a trunk up to {{convert|1-2|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} in diameter and a rounded or irregular crown. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]], which can be peeled in strips, is dark grayish-brown. The [[leaves]] are of two forms, juvenile needle-like leaves {{Convert|5–14|mm|frac=4}} long and 1 mm wide on seedlings, and adult scale-leaves 1–2 mm long on older plants with a green to blue-green color; they are arranged in opposite decussate pairs or whorls of three. It is largely [[monoecious]], but some individual plants are [[dioecious]]. The female [[conifer cone|cones]] are [[Juniper berry|berrylike]], 6–14 mm in diameter, orange-brown, occasionally with a pinkish waxy bloom, and contain 3–8 [[seed]]s; they are mature in about 18 months, and are mainly dispersed by birds. The male cones are 2–4 mm long, and shed their pollen in early spring, which is then dispersed by wind.

==Taxonomy==
The Phoenician juniper was historically treated as a [[species complex]], encompassing a range of morphological and ecological variations often classified as [[subspecies]] or [[Variety (botany)|varieties]]. This traditional view recognized a broadly distributed species throughout the Mediterranean basin and Macaronesia.
Contemporary genetic<ref name=Sánchez-Gómez2018>{{cite journal | doi=10.1007/s13595-018-0741-7 | title=Genetic structure and phylogeography of ''Juniperus phoenicea'' complex throughout Mediterranean and Macaronesian regions: Different stories in one | date=2018 | last1=Sánchez-Gómez | first1=Pedro | last2=Jiménez | first2=Juan F. | last3=Cánovas | first3=Jose Luis | last4=Vera | first4=Juan Bautista | last5=Hensen | first5=Isabell | last6=Aouissat | first6=Miloud | journal=Annals of Forest Science | volume=75 | issue=3 | hdl=10481/87512 | hdl-access=free }}</ref> and morphological<ref name=Mazur2018>{{cite journal | doi=10.1080/14772000.2018.1439120 | title=Taxonomic and geographic differentiation of ''Juniperus phoenicea agg.'' based on cone, seed, and needle characteristics | date=2018 | last1=Mazur | first1=Małgorzata | last2=Zielińska | first2=Monika | last3=Boratyńska | first3=Krystyna | last4=Romo | first4=Angel | last5=Salva-Catarineu | first5=Montserrat | last6=Marcysiak | first6=Katarzyna | last7=Boratyński | first7=Adam | journal=Systematics and Biodiversity | volume=16 | issue=5 | pages=469–482 }}</ref> studies have necessitated a significant revision of this species complex. These phylogenetic analyses supported a clear differentiation among the previously grouped populations, leading to the separation of the complex into three distinct, recognized species:<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ipni.org |title=IPNI |last1= |first1= |last2= |first2= |date=|website=International Plant Names Index |publisher=The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Harvard University Herbaria & Libraries and Australian National Herbarium |access-date=30 September 2025 |quote=}}</ref>
*''Juniperus phoenicea'' <small>L.</small> s.s. ([[sensu|sensu stricto]]): This species now typically refers to the populations found primarily in the western [[Mediterranean region]].
*''[[Juniperus turbinata]]'' <small>Guss.</small>: This species is recognized for populations distributed across the Mediterranean and western [[Saudi Arabia]]. It is often distinguished by its more turbinate (top-shaped) cones and differences in foliage.
*''[[Juniperus canariensis]]'' <small>Guyot & Mathou</small>: This species is endemic to the [[Macaronesia|Macaronesian archipelagos]] (primarily the [[Canary Islands]] and [[Madeira]]). Its distinction is strongly supported by genetic divergence reflecting its long-term isolation in these island environments.
This taxonomic reclassification provides a more accurate reflection of the evolutionary history and biogeographical segregation within the taxon, highlighting the distinct adaptive trajectories of the three newly accepted species.

==Distribution and habitat==
The species is primarily distributed in the Western [[Mediterranean region]] and its core range is concentrated in [[Spain]] (principally the eastern provinces) and Southern [[France]]. Additional, often isolated, occurrences have been reported in other areas of the Western Mediterranean, including the [[Sierra de Tramuntana]] in [[Mallorca]] and [[Cabo Espichel]] in [[Portugal]]. In [[Italy]], it is found in the western [[Maritime Alps]], and the [[Apuan Alps]], and has also been reported from [[Monte Albo]] in [[Sardinia]].<ref name=Boratynski2024>{{cite journal |last1=Boratyński |first1=A. |last2=Salva-Catarineu |first2=M. |last3=Marcysiak |first3=K. |last4=Mazur |first4=M. |last5=Romo |first5=A. |last6=Minissale |first6=P. |last7=Tan |first7=K. |last8=Iszkuło |first8=G. |last9=Witkowski |first9=R. |last10=Mazur |first10=A. |date=2024 |title=Biology and ecology of the ''Juniperus phoenicea'' – ''J. turbinata'' – ''J. canariensis'' complex I. Taxonomy, structure and distribution |journal=Dendrobiology |volume=92 |pages=1–31 |doi=10.12657/denbio.092.001 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

This juniper generally occurs at elevations ranging from 50 to 100 m to about 1,600–1,800 m, with the largest concentration of localities found between 400 and 1,200 m. This distribution reflects its preference for inland, rocky, and sub-mountainous habitats, often on calcareous soils. The highest documented elevations for the species are 1,900 m in the [[Sierra Nevada (Spain)|Sierra Nevada]] and 1,970 m in the [[Sierra Mágina]], both located in Spain.<ref name=Boratynski2024/>

==Ecology==
The species prefers a hot, arid climate with a lot of light, and grows on rocky or sandy ground. Its preferred soil is calcareous with a [[Soil pH|pH]] between 7.7 and 7.9 (moderately basic), but could also be silicate. Despite having a shallow root system,<ref name="Runeburg1960e" /> it can survive with as little as {{Convert|200|mm|abbr=on|frac=2}} of rain per year. It can often be found forming scrubs and thickets with other species.<ref name="Caudullo-2016">{{cite book |first1=G. |last1=Caudullo |first2=D. |last2=de Rigo |year=2016 |chapter=''Juniperus phoenicea'' in Europe: distribution, habitat, usage and threats |chapter-url=https://forest.jrc.ec.europa.eu/media/atlas/Juniperus_phoenicea.pdf |title=European Atlas of Forest Tree Species |url=http://forest.jrc.ec.europa.eu/european-atlas-of-forest-tree-species/ |publisher=European Commission }}</ref> In its natural range of France and Spain, ''J. phoenicea'' has a generational life of 25 years, and is considered a stable species on the 2016 IUCN [[Red List of Threatened Species]].<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Boratyński |first=Adam |last2=Salvà-Catarineu |first2=Montserrat |last3=Marcysiak |first3=Katarzyna |last4=Mazur |first4=Małgorzata |last5=Romo |first5=Ángel |last6=Minissale |first6=Pietro |last7=Tan |first7=Kit |last8=Iszkuło |first8=Grzegorz |last9=Witkowski |first9=Radosław |last10=Mazur |first10=Andrzej |date=2025 |title=Biology and ecology of Juniperus phoenicea – J. turbinata – J. canariensis complex II. Genetics, physiology, ecology |url=https://www.idpan.poznan.pl/pl/vol-93/93-18-41 |journal=Dendrobiology |volume=93 |pages=18–41 |doi=10.12657/denbio.093.002 |issn=1641-1307|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Its habitat in coastal areas is most threatened by the presence of humans, both settled and touring. Humans also plant not-naturally-present plants such as pines, black locust, French tamarisk, desert false Indigo, American agave, tree of heaven, and some succulent plants from South Africa. The purpose of this is usually to stabilize the dunes, but these outside plants interfere with the natural vegetation. It is also threatened easily by fires, because it is quite flammable and does not regenerate well. This makes it necessary to plant new organisms after a fire has damaged the others.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1080/15324982.2015.1090499 |title=Ecological assessment of populations of ''Juniperus phoenicea'' L. In the Al-Akhdar mountainous landscape of Libya |journal=Arid Land Research and Management |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=269–89 |year=2016 |last1=Kabiel |first1=Hanan F. |last2=Hegazy |first2=Ahmad K. |last3=Lovett-Doust |first3=Lesley |last4=Al-Rowaily |first4=Saud L. |last5=Al Borki |first5=Abd El-Nasser S. |bibcode=2016ALRM...30..269K |s2cid=130032990 |url=https://portal.arid.my/Publications/39192bf7-a9ab-4e4b-8d42-218bf47c3445.pdf}}</ref>

==Uses==
{{Further|Juniper berry}}

Juniper berries are used as a [[seasoning]] in cooking or in [[alcoholic beverage]]s,<ref name="Caudullo-2016"/> particularly to flavor [[gin]].<ref name="drugs">{{cite web |title=Juniper |url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/juniper.html |publisher=Drugs.com |access-date=22 February 2019 |date=2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last= Cornish |first= Chloe|date=  19 November 2021|title= "In tumultuous Lebanon, a bright spot in . . . gin-making" |url= https://www.ft.com/content/781ba5e6-28f1-4261-8fdf-648f7c5128c5|work= The Financial Times|access-date= 1 August 2021|archive-url=https://archive.today/20211120062857/https://www.ft.com/content/781ba5e6-28f1-4261-8fdf-648f7c5128c5|archive-date= 2021-11-20|url-status=live}}</ref> Juniper berries have also been used in [[traditional medicine]] for different conditions, although there is no [[evidence-based medicine|high-quality clinical evidence]] that it has any effect.<ref name=drugs/> Although [[extract]]s of juniper berries or [[wood tar]] have been used as an [[aroma]]{{Snd}}particularly for [[cosmetics]]{{Snd}}the safety of using [[topical medication|ointments]] manufactured from ''J. phoenicea'' and related species has not been adequately demonstrated, according to a 2001 review.<ref name="ijt">{{cite journal | title=Final report on the safety assessment of ''Juniperus communis'' extract, ''Juniperus oxycedrus'' extract, ''Juniperus oxycedrus'' tar, ''Juniperus phoenicea'' extract, and ''Juniperus virginiana'' extract | journal=International Journal of Toxicology | volume=20 Suppl 2 | issue=2 | year=2001 | issn=1091-5818 | pmid=11558640 | pages=41–56 | doi=10.1080/10915810160233758| s2cid=40114722 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Juniper extracts used topically may cause skin [[allergic reaction]]s, and should be avoided during pregnancy.<ref name=drugs/>

The tree's [[essential oil]] is especially rich in the tricyclic [[sesquiterpene]] [[thujopsene]].<ref name="pubchem">{{cite web | title=Pubchem Compound Database; CID 442402: Thujopsene | publisher=Pubchem, National Center for Biotechnology Information, US National Library of Medicine | url=https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/442402|date=16 February 2019 | access-date=22 February 2019}}</ref> The [[heartwood]] contains an estimated 2.2% of thujopsene; this explains the superior natural durability of the wood itself.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Lykidis | first1=Charalampos | last2=Bak | first2=Miklos | author3-link=George Mantanis | last3=Mantanis | first3=George I. | title=Biological resistance of Phoenician juniper wood | journal=Wood Material Science & Engineering | volume=19 | issue=1 | date=2024-01-02 | issn=1748-0272 | doi=10.1080/17480272.2023.2221657 | pages=1–5}}</ref> The biochemist Jarl Runeburg noted in 1960 that ''J. phoenicea'' appears to be the most convenient source of thujopsene so far encountered."<ref name="Runeburg1960e">{{cite journal |doi=10.3891/acta.chem.scand.14-1995 |title=The Chemistry of the Natural Order Cupressales. XXXI. Heartwood Constituents of ''Juniperus phoenicea'' L. |journal=Acta Chemica Scandinavica |volume=14 |pages=1995–8 |year=1960 |last1=Runeberg |first1=Jarl |last2=Gramstad |first2=Thor |last3=Larsson |first3=Lennart |last4=Dodson |first4=R. M. |doi-access=free }}</ref> Juniper wood is used for small manufactured objects and [[inlay]] works in [[carpentry]], and in building construction in Africa where it is mainly used for fuel and producing [[charcoal]].<ref name="Caudullo-2016" />

==Culture==
It is the vegetable symbol of the island of [[El Hierro]].<ref>{{cite act|type=Ley|index=7/1991|date=30 April 1991|title=Símbolos de la naturaleza para las Islas Canarias|trans-title=Natural Symbols for the Canary Islands|pages=20946–20497|url=https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1991-16276|language=es|via=[[Boletín Oficial del Estado|BOE]]|volume=151}}</ref>
